facts.title: Named For Making Water
facts.text: Hydrogen's name comes from the Greek words hydro (water) and genes (forming), meaning 'water-former.' The French chemist Antoine Lavoisier coined it in 1783 after showing that burning the gas produces pure water. Earlier, in 1766, Henry Cavendish had isolated it and called it 'inflammable air' without realizing it was a distinct element.

facts.title: The Lightest Of All
facts.text: With just one proton and one electron, hydrogen is the lightest and simplest element in the universe. A single hydrogen atom has a mass of about 1.67 x 10^-27 kilograms, roughly 1,836 times lighter than nothing you can hold. Because of this it tops the periodic table and is the only element whose most common form has no neutron at all.

facts.title: Three Quarters Of The Cosmos
facts.text: Hydrogen makes up about 75 percent of all ordinary (baryonic) matter in the universe by mass. It was the first element to form, appearing just minutes after the Big Bang during a phase called Big Bang nucleosynthesis. Stars like our Sun shine by fusing hydrogen nuclei into helium in their cores.

facts.title: It Has Named Twins
facts.text: Hydrogen is the only element whose isotopes have their own names: protium (no neutrons), deuterium (one neutron), and tritium (two neutrons). Deuterium, discovered by Harold Urey in 1931, earned him the 1934 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. 'Heavy water' made with deuterium is used to control reactions in some nuclear reactors.

facts.title: The Powerhouse Of The Sun
facts.text: Every second, the Sun fuses roughly 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium, releasing the energy that lights and warms our planet. This proton-proton fusion converts a tiny fraction of mass directly into energy, following Einstein's E=mc squared. The same process is what scientists are trying to recreate on Earth in fusion reactors like ITER in France.

facts.title: A Metal Hidden In Giants
facts.text: Under the crushing pressures deep inside Jupiter and Saturn, hydrogen is squeezed into a strange state called metallic hydrogen that conducts electricity like a metal. Researchers believe this liquid metallic hydrogen generates these planets' powerful magnetic fields. Creating it in the lab requires pressures of millions of atmospheres and remains one of physics' hardest challenges.

facts.title: Fuel With Only Water Exhaust
facts.text: When hydrogen burns or reacts in a fuel cell, its only by-product is water, making it an attractive clean energy carrier. Hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles convert the gas into electricity to drive motors, emitting nothing but water vapor. The catch is that most hydrogen today is made from natural gas, so 'green' hydrogen from renewable-powered water splitting is a major research goal.

facts.title: Feeding The World's Crops
facts.text: Hydrogen is essential to the Haber-Bosch process, which combines it with nitrogen to make ammonia for fertilizer. Developed by Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch in the early 1900s, this reaction supports food production for roughly half the world's population. It is also one of industry's biggest energy users, consuming a large share of global hydrogen output.

facts.title: The Bond That Shapes Life
facts.text: The 'hydrogen bond,' a weak attraction involving a hydrogen atom, is one of the most important forces in biology. It holds the two strands of your DNA's double helix together and gives water its unusually high boiling point and surface tension. Without hydrogen bonds, proteins could not fold into their working shapes and life as we know it could not exist.

facts.title: Coldest Liquid On The Launchpad
facts.text: Liquid hydrogen, used as rocket fuel, must be kept colder than minus 253 degrees Celsius, just above absolute zero. NASA's Space Shuttle and the Saturn V upper stages burned liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen for tremendous thrust. Hydrogen also has the highest energy content per kilogram of any common fuel, which is why rockets prize it despite the difficulty of storing it.
